In the second-year hostel in Manipal, Dhruv had been the boy who slept at 3 a.m. and missed 8 a.m. lectures. In September he decided to change it himself.
He taped a chart to his cupboard: bed by 12:30, up by 7:30, two hours of study before lunch. Every day he coloured a box green or red.
The first week was mostly red. The second, half and half. By the fifth week, the chart was almost all green.
His roommate Jyoti's brother, visiting, asked about the chart. Dhruv pointed at the green boxes. “I did those.”
His attendance went from 60% to 92%. His first internal marks came back: two As, where last year there had been Cs.
He stood in front of the chart that night, feeling something new. Not luck. Not someone else's plan. He had written this.

qa.q: What was Dhruv's attendance after the change?
qa.a: His attendance went from 60% to 92%.

qa.q: How did Dhruv feel standing in front of the chart?
qa.a: He felt proud and newly confident, sensing that he, not luck, had made the change.

qa.q: Why did recording progress on a chart help Dhruv?
qa.a: The green boxes gave visible evidence that his actions caused the results, building his sense of being in charge.

qa.q: How might Jyoti's brother see the chart?
qa.a: He might be curious and a little impressed at how much Dhruv had changed by himself.

grounding: The passage shows a student deciding to fix sleep and study schedules, recording progress, and gaining confidence as the author of the change.

Dear Abhinav,

You asked how I pulled my grades up this year. I want to tell you properly, because it surprised me.

Last year I blamed everything: the timetable, my roommate's snoring, the professors. Then in January I decided to take charge of two things only: sleep and study hours.

I made a simple sheet. Sleep time, wake time, hours studied. I filled it in every night for four months, even the bad days.

The sheet changed how I saw myself. When I slept by midnight, my study hours doubled. When I studied four days in a row, my quiz marks went up. I could see the line going up because of what I did.

I'm not saying luck doesn't matter. But I've never felt this much like I'm driving.

Divyansh

qa.q: What did Divyansh record on the sheet?
qa.a: Divyansh recorded sleep time, wake time and hours studied.

qa.q: How does Divyansh feel about the change?
qa.a: Divyansh feels surprised and confident, like driving instead of being carried along.

qa.q: Why did the sheet help more than good intentions?
qa.a: It showed clear links between Divyansh's actions and results, teaching that Divyansh authors some outcomes.

qa.q: How might Abhinav feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Abhinav might feel encouraged and curious to try a similar sheet.

grounding: The letter shows a student taking charge of sleep and study, recording progress, and feeling like the author of the improvement.

I'm not saying it's all me. But I've never had proof before that what I do actually changes things. That notebook is proof. I feel, I don't know, like I have a steering wheel now.

In Karad, Chandrika, sixteen, sat on the steps outside the temple long after the evening aarti.
Her friend Eshaan had been caught bunking school to hang around the bus stand with older boys. His father had been called in.
Chandrika kept going over it. She had seen him skip on Monday and hadn't said anything. On Tuesday she'd been too busy with her project to walk home with him. If she had, maybe he wouldn't have gone.
“It's my fault,” she told her mother at dinner.
Her mother put down the ladle. “Did you tell him to bunk?”
“No.”
“Did you take him to the bus stand?”
“No, but…”
“Then it's his choice. You can be sad for him. You can talk to him. But you can't carry what he chose, beta.”
Chandrika nodded slowly, but the heavy feeling in her chest stayed a while longer.

qa.q: Where had Eshaan been hanging around when he bunked school?
qa.a: He had been hanging around the bus stand with older boys.

In Melbourne, Chidi, fifteen, sat in the school library, not reading. His friend Tuan had been caught copying answers in the maths exam and was suspended for two days.
Chidi kept replaying it. Last week Tuan had asked to see his homework, and Chidi had said yes. If he'd said no, maybe Tuan wouldn't have thought copying was fine. Maybe it had started with him.
When the librarian, Ms Patel, asked if he was okay, he blurted, “It's my fault Tuan cheated.”
She sat down. “Did you give him your exam answers?”
“No. Just homework, once.”
“Did you tell him to copy?”
“No.”
“Then you're carrying something that isn't yours. You can be a good friend. You can tell him what you think. But you're not in charge of his choices.”
Chidi let out a long breath. It was hard to believe.

Nikita's first-year rank came out on a day when the hostel Wi-Fi was down and it was pouring in Bhopal. She read it on a friend's phone under the mess awning: 212 out of 400.
Her roommate Parul had got 48. For a moment Nikita wanted to say, “She got lucky, she went to that famous school.” For another moment she wanted to say, “I'm just stupid.”
She sat on the wet bench and tried to think clearly. Parul's school had given her a head start in maths; that was luck. The physics paper had been unusually hard; that was chance too. But Nikita had also skipped the last two weeks of revision for her cousin's wedding. That was a choice.
She wrote it on the back of her hand in pen: Luck: school, paper. Me: revision.
That night she borrowed Parul's maths notes and made a revision timetable for the next semester.

Vinita got into the college she wanted in Chennai, and at first she told everyone it was because she worked so hard. Then her friend Charu didn't get in, though Charu had worked just as hard.
One evening in the hostel canteen, Charu said quietly, “Maybe I'm just not good enough.”
Vinita thought about it. She had studied every day for a year. That was true. But she had also had a tutor her parents could pay for, a quiet room at home, and the English paper had been on a topic she happened to love.
“Charu, I worked hard. You worked hard. But I also had some luck you didn't. A tutor. An easy essay topic.”
Charu blinked. “So it wasn't all you?”
“No. And it wasn't all you either. What can you change for next year's entrance?”
They sat and made a list: mock tests, a study group. The things they could actually move.

qa.q: At what point in the story did young Vidya start to feel safe trying?
qa.a: When the new teacher said she cared about trying more than cleverness.

qa.q: How might young Vidya's father have felt if he knew his praise made her afraid?

passage:
It was the night before the school science fair, and the power in the colony kept flickering. Vandana, eleven, sat at the table with her aunt Uma.
Everyone called Vandana “our little scientist.” Uma always said, “You're so smart, you'll win easily.”
Her teacher had suggested a hard project: building a water filter and testing it. Vandana had chosen instead to make a poster about the planets, which she already knew by heart.
“Why not the filter?” Uma asked.
Vandana shrugged. “What if it doesn't work? Then everyone will see I'm not that smart.”
Uma paused, the torch in her hand. She thought of all the times she'd said “so smart.”
“Vandana, I think I've been saying the wrong thing. I'm proud when you try hard things. Even if they don't work.”
Vandana looked at the planets poster, then away, cheeks hot.

qa.q: What hard project had the teacher suggested?
qa.a: Building a water filter and testing it.

qa.q: Why did Vandana choose the planets poster?
qa.a: She was afraid that a failed filter would show she isn't smart, so the safe project protected her label.

qa.q: What did Uma change in how she praised Vandana?
qa.a: She said she is proud when Vandana tries hard things even if they fail, praising effort rather than being smart.

qa.q: How might Uma feel realising her praise played a part?
qa.a: Uma seems regretful and thoughtful, recognising that “so smart” made risk feel dangerous.

grounding: The passage shows a child repeatedly called smart choosing a safe project to protect the label, and an aunt rethinking her praise.

passage:
In the Nandgaon village school, Farhan, ten, was stuck sharing 36 mangoes among 4 families. He drew mangoes. Too many. He counted in fours on his fingers and lost count. Then he remembered the multiplication table on the wall and worked backwards: 4 times 9 is 36.
Bhavna Ma'am came by and looked at his slate, covered in crossed-out mangoes and finger marks.
She didn't say “clever boy.” She said, “You tried three different ways. When drawing didn't work, you changed your plan. That's how you got it.”
Farhan looked at his slate as if seeing it for the first time.
The next day there was a hard sum on the board, and he put his hand up first. “Ma'am, can I try it? I'll try a different way if it doesn't work.”

qa.q: How many mangoes were being shared?
qa.a: 36 mangoes were being shared among 4 families.

qa.q: How did Farhan feel when Bhavna Ma'am described what he did?
qa.a: He felt surprised and proud, seeing his messy slate as proof that his changing strategies worked.

qa.q: Why was Bhavna Ma'am's praise effective?
qa.a: She praised his specific strategies and persistence instead of cleverness, which taught him that ability grows with effort.

qa.q: How might Bhavna Ma'am feel seeing Farhan volunteer for the hard sum?
qa.a: She would likely feel pleased and encouraged that her praise made him seek a challenge.

grounding: The passage shows a teacher praising a child's changing strategies rather than cleverness, and the child starting to seek challenges.

passage:
In a school in Mexico City, Omar, nine, was building a bridge from paper and tape that had to hold ten coins. His first bridge collapsed at three coins. His second held five.
He was about to give up when he noticed his friend's bridge had folded paper, like a fan. He tried folding his. It held eight coins. Then he added a second layer. It held twelve.
His teacher, Ms Camila, crouched down. “Omar, I watched you. When the flat bridge fell, you didn't quit. You looked at a different design, tried folding, then added a layer. That's why it worked.”
Omar grinned. “So I'm good at bridges?”
“You're good at trying new ways,” she said. “That's better.”
On Friday, when they had to build a tower, Omar picked the hardest design on the sheet.

qa.q: How many coins did Omar's final bridge hold?
qa.a: It held twelve coins.

qa.q: How did Omar feel when Ms Camila explained what he did?
qa.a: He felt proud and happy, grinning at the specific praise of his methods.

qa.q: Why did Ms Camila's praise support challenge seeking?
qa.a: She named his strategies and persistence rather than a talent, so Omar learned that effort and new methods pay off.

qa.q: How might Ms Camila feel when Omar picks the hardest design on Friday?
qa.a: She would probably feel delighted that her process praise made him more willing to take on challenges.

grounding: The passage shows a teacher praising a child's changing methods rather than talent, and the child choosing harder challenges afterwards.

passage:
At the Saturday chess club in the community hall, Alka, eleven, had lost three games in a row to Ria. In the fourth game she sat very still, thinking longer before each move. She tried castling early. She protected her queen. She lost again, but only after forty moves.
Coach Naveen came over as she packed her pieces. “Alka, can I tell you what I saw? In game one you moved fast. In game four you slowed down, you planned your castling and you guarded your queen. That's why it lasted forty moves.”
Alka frowned. “But I still lost.”
“You did. But you changed your strategy, and it worked better. That's how players get stronger.”
Alka looked at the board. Then she walked over to Ria. “Can we play again next Saturday? I want to try something else.”

qa.q: How many moves did Alka's fourth game last?
qa.a: It lasted forty moves.

qa.q: How did Alka feel when she said “But I still lost”?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and a bit discouraged, focused on the loss rather than her progress.

qa.q: Why was Coach Naveen's feedback effective?
qa.a: He named specific changes in her strategy and linked them to the better result, showing that skill grows with effort.

qa.q: How might Ria see Alka asking for a rematch?
qa.a: Ria might feel respected and a little surprised that Alka wants to play again after four losses.

grounding: The passage shows a coach praising a child's strategy changes rather than talent, and the child seeking another challenge.

passage:
Mei had always drawn a little in the margins of her notes, at her school in Singapore. In Year 10 art, the first project was a portrait. Hers looked flat, with the eyes too far apart.
Her classmate Noa's portrait looked almost like a photograph.
Mei put her pencil down. “I'm just not creative. Some people have it, some don't.”
“I've been drawing every day since I was ten,” Noa said. “My first faces looked like potatoes.”
“That's different. You're naturally good.”
The next week Mei chose the written option instead of the art project. When the art teacher asked why, she said, “I'm not an art person.”
She stopped drawing in her margins too. The notebook pages stayed clean and white.

qa.q: What was the first Year 10 art project?
qa.a: A portrait.

qa.q: Why did Mei put her pencil down after seeing Noa's portrait?
qa.a: She felt discouraged and inadequate, believing creativity is fixed and she simply doesn't have it.

qa.q: What could the art teacher say to help Mei?
qa.a: The teacher could show how skills like spacing the eyes can be learned step by step, and invite her to practise one small thing.

qa.q: How does Noa see the portrait skill?
qa.a: Noa sees that skill as the result of years of daily practice, starting from faces that looked like potatoes.

grounding: The passage shows a teenager deciding she is just not creative after one weak portrait, turning her current level into a permanent limit.

passage:
In the art room of the Kanpur girls' school, Sonali Ma'am handed back the still-life sketches. Rukmini, fifteen, looked at hers: a lopsided jug, wobbly shadows.
“I'm just not creative, Ma'am. Some people are born with it.”
“Rukmini, this is your third sketch ever.”
“And it's bad.”
“It's early.”
Rukmini shook her head. “My sister's an artist. She got all the talent. I got maths.” She pushed the sketch into her bag, crumpled.
For the rest of term, she chose the easiest tasks: tracing, colouring inside printed lines. When they had to draw from life again, she said she had a headache.
Sonali Ma'am watched her, frowning. She'd seen Rukmini's first sketch and her third side by side. The third was better. Rukmini just hadn't looked.

qa.q: What did Rukmini sketch?
qa.a: She sketched a still life with a jug.

qa.q: Why did Rukmini crumple her sketch into her bag?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and discouraged, believing talent is fixed and that her sister got it all.

qa.q: What could Sonali Ma'am do next to help Rukmini?
qa.a: Show Rukmini her first and third sketches side by side, so she can see she is already improving.

qa.q: How does Sonali Ma'am see Rukmini's drawing?
qa.a: Sonali Ma'am sees real improvement from the first sketch to the third and feels concerned that Rukmini hasn't noticed.

grounding: The passage shows a teenager who is weak at drawing deciding she is not creative and avoiding it, turning her current level into a fixed limit.

passage:
Dear Nirmala Didi,

You asked why I dropped the art elective. The truth is, I'm just not a creative person. You got those genes, not me.

On the first day we had to draw a hand. Everyone else's looked like a hand. Mine looked like a glove full of sticks. The teacher said it was “a start.” I knew what that meant.

So I switched to accountancy. I'm good with numbers. That's who I am.

Sometimes, though, in accountancy class, I doodle little birds in the corner of the page. They're not very good. I cross them out before anyone sees.

Anyway, how's your exhibition going? Send me pictures.

Rajni

qa.q: What did Rajni have to draw on the first day?
qa.a: A hand.

qa.q: How does Rajni feel about drawing, based on the crossed-out birds?
qa.a: Rajni seems to still enjoy drawing but feels embarrassed and inadequate, believing creativity is a fixed trait Rajni lacks.

qa.q: What could Nirmala Didi say in reply that might help?
qa.a: That Nirmala Didi's own early drawings were rough too, and that skill grows with practice, inviting Rajni to keep doodling without judging.

qa.q: How might Nirmala Didi feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Nirmala Didi might feel sad and a little guilty that her talent made Rajni feel it was out of reach.

grounding: The letter shows a teenager who struggled with one drawing deciding creativity is fixed, turning a current level into a permanent limit.

passage:
You want to know why I stopped going to the design club, Simran? Okay. It's embarrassing.
I'm Parul. There's this girl in my batch, Aarti. First year, she walked in and designed the whole fest poster in two days. Everyone went crazy over it. The professors use her work as an example.
And I felt sick. Not happy for her. Sick. Like, what's the point of me? She's just born with it. I'll never be at that level.
Every time I see her work now, I feel like I've lost something. Like her talent takes something away from mine.
So I stopped going. I tell people I'm busy.
I know that's stupid. I know she probably practises a lot. But in the moment, it just feels like the gap is fixed. Like she's on one side and I'm on the other, forever.

qa.q: How long did Aarti take to design the fest poster?
qa.a: Aarti designed the whole fest poster in two days.

qa.q: How does Parul feel when seeing Aarti's work?
qa.a: Parul feels envious and threatened, as if Aarti's talent takes something away from Parul's own.

qa.q: What could Parul try instead of avoiding the club?
qa.a: Ask Aarti how she practises, or go back and work on one small skill, treating Aarti's success as a guide rather than a loss.

qa.q: How might Simran respond to Parul's confession?
qa.a: Simran might feel sympathetic and gently point out that Aarti's skill likely came from practice, not destiny.

grounding: The monologue shows a student seeing a peer excel, deciding the gap is fixed, and feeling threatened rather than inspired.

passage:
Week 1: Indu, nineteen, was placed in the same coding team as Kunal, who solved every problem before she'd finished reading it. Indu smiled at him in the lab, but inside she felt a hot sting.
Week 3: At night Indu lay awake thinking: he's a natural, I'm not. Every time the professor praised Kunal, she felt smaller. She stopped asking questions in class so no one would compare them.
Week 5: Kunal offered to help her with a bug. She said, “I'm fine,” too quickly. Later she found out he'd been coding since he was twelve and still spent every weekend practising.
Indu sat with that for a long time. The gap wasn't destiny. It was seven years and a lot of weekends. The sting was still there, but smaller.

qa.q: Since what age had Kunal been coding?
qa.a: He had been coding since he was twelve.

qa.q: How did Indu feel when the professor praised Kunal?
qa.a: She felt envious and smaller, as if his success were her loss.

qa.q: What changed Indu's view in week 5?
qa.a: Learning about Kunal's years of practice showed her the gap came from effort, not destiny.

qa.q: How might Kunal feel when Indu refuses his help too quickly?
qa.a: Kunal might feel confused and a little rejected, since he only wanted to help.

grounding: The three beats show a student envying a talented peer, seeing the gap as destiny, and beginning to see it as practice instead.

passage:
Manoj, you say your roommate is so gifted at music that you've stopped playing your own guitar. Let me, your Zeenat Khala, tell you about Rehana.
When I was twenty, in Hyderabad, Rehana and I both sang in the college choir. Her voice was like honey. Everyone turned to look when she sang.
I couldn't bear it. I felt like every compliment she got was taken from me. I decided she was born with it, and I was not. I stopped going to practice.
Years later I met her at a wedding. She told me she used to wake up at five every day to do voice exercises before college. Five, every day.
I had thought her voice was destiny. It was her mornings.
I wasted years feeling robbed by her. Don't do that, beta. Watch how your roommate practises.

qa.q: At what time did Rehana wake up for voice exercises?
qa.a: She woke up at five every day.

qa.q: How did young Zeenat feel when Rehana was praised?
qa.a: She felt envious and robbed, as if every compliment for Rehana were taken from her.

qa.q: At what point in the story did Zeenat's view of Rehana's talent change?
qa.a: At the wedding years later, when she learned about Rehana's daily five o'clock practice.

qa.q: How might Rehana have felt if she knew Zeenat left the choir because of her?
qa.a: Rehana might have felt sad and surprised, since she was only practising, not competing.

grounding: The aunt's memory shows a student seeing a peer excel, deciding the gap is destiny and feeling robbed rather than inspired.
